meta.name: Configuring Windows Server Hybrid Advanced Services (AZ-801)
meta.notes: Initial pack — 12 questions across the AZ-801 exam domains: securing Windows Server on-premises and hybrid infrastructures, implementing and managing high availability, disaster recovery, server and workload migration, and monitoring and troubleshooting Windows Server environments.

questions.question: Your security team wants domain controllers to refuse to cache the credentials of administrative accounts if they are ever logged on to lower-trust member servers, so that a compromised member server cannot replay or extract those credentials. Which Active Directory feature should you implement to protect privileged accounts in this way?
options: Add the privileged accounts to the Protected Users global security group
Enable Credential Guard with virtualization-based security on every member server
Configure a fine-grained password policy that increases the password length for administrators
Enable Kerberos armoring (Flexible Authentication Secure Tunneling) on every member server
questions.explanation: Membership in the Protected Users group hardens privileged accounts at the directory level: NTLM authentication, DES and RC4 encryption in Kerberos, unconstrained delegation, and the caching of cached credentials are all blocked, and Kerberos ticket lifetimes are capped at 4 hours. Credential Guard protects LSA secrets on the local machine but does not change what AD itself returns. Fine-grained password policies only affect password complexity. Kerberos armoring (FAST) protects the Kerberos exchange but not the broader credential surface that Protected Users covers.

questions.question: A regulated workload running on Windows Server 2022 must be able to run only an explicit allow-list of binaries — including PowerShell scripts and MSI installers — even if an administrator with local privileges attempts to launch an unsigned tool. The policy must be enforced by code integrity at the kernel and user-mode layers, not by a user-space service that an administrator can stop. Which control should you deploy?
options: AppLocker rules enforced through Group Policy
Software Restriction Policies (SRP)
User Account Control (UAC) at the highest prompt level
Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies
questions.explanation: Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) is enforced by the kernel through the code-integrity subsystem and cannot be bypassed by stopping a service — that is its main advantage over AppLocker, which runs as the AppIDSvc user-mode service and can be disabled by a local administrator. SRP is deprecated. UAC controls elevation prompts, not which binaries are allowed to execute.

questions.question: You manage roughly 200 on-premises and multi-cloud servers that are connected to Azure with Azure Arc. The compliance team wants Microsoft Defender for Cloud to perform agentless and agent-based threat detection, file integrity monitoring, and vulnerability assessment against those Arc-enabled servers. Which Defender for Cloud plan must be enabled to deliver this coverage on Arc-enabled servers?
options: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Plan 1 only
Microsoft Defender for Identity
Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps
Microsoft Defender for Servers Plan 2
questions.explanation: Defender for Servers Plan 2 is the Defender for Cloud plan that targets servers — including Azure Arc-enabled machines outside Azure — and delivers Defender for Endpoint integration, file integrity monitoring, just-in-time VM access, adaptive application controls, and the integrated vulnerability assessment (formerly Qualys, now MDVM). Defender for Endpoint Plan 1 is the EDR product alone, without the Defender for Cloud server-protection extras. Defender for Cloud Apps is a CASB; Defender for Identity protects AD DS by analysing domain controller traffic, not general server posture.

questions.question: You are designing a 4-node Storage Spaces Direct (S2D) hyper-converged failover cluster that will run virtual machines on Windows Server 2022. The cluster needs to tolerate the loss of any single node and any single drive without losing data or quorum, and the witness must remain available even if the on-premises datacentre WAN is degraded. Which witness configuration best meets these requirements?
options: Configure a disk witness on a shared SAS array attached to all four nodes
Configure a file share witness on a server in the same rack as the cluster
Configure a cloud witness backed by an Azure storage account
Disable the witness because a 4-node cluster already has an even node count
questions.explanation: An S2D cluster does not use shared SAS storage — each node owns its disks — so a disk witness is not supported. A file share witness in the same rack would fail along with the cluster if that rack lost power. A cloud witness uses a tiny blob in an Azure storage account, has no compute footprint, and remains reachable as long as outbound HTTPS to Azure works, making it the recommended quorum witness for clusters that need site-resilient arbitration. Even-node clusters always need a witness to avoid split-brain.

questions.question: Two Windows Server 2022 Hyper-V hosts in different datacentres replicate critical VMs to each other using Hyper-V Replica. Business requirements state that, after a regional outage, you must be able to fail VMs over to the secondary site with a Recovery Point Objective of no more than 30 seconds. Which replication frequency option should you configure for those VMs?
options: 30 seconds
5 minutes
15 minutes
1 hour
questions.explanation: Hyper-V Replica supports three replication intervals: 30 seconds, 5 minutes, and 15 minutes. To meet a 30-second RPO the replication frequency must be set to 30 seconds — 5 or 15 minutes would risk losing more data than the RPO allows. 1 hour is not a supported Hyper-V Replica interval. For tighter RPOs than 30 seconds you would use Storage Replica synchronous replication or an Azure Site Recovery configuration with shorter snapshots.

questions.question: You need to provide crash-consistent, application-consistent, and bare-metal recovery for an on-premises Windows Server 2022 file server, with backups stored off-site in Azure and immutable for 90 days against ransomware and rogue administrators. Which combination should you deploy?
options: Azure Backup MARS agent only, with local soft delete enabled
Azure File Sync with cloud tiering and a 90-day file-version retention policy
Robocopy to an SMB share in an Azure storage account, scheduled with Task Scheduler
Microsoft Azure Backup Server (MABS) with a Recovery Services vault that has immutability and soft delete enabled
questions.explanation: Microsoft Azure Backup Server (MABS) brings application-aware, VSS-based backup of Windows workloads, system state, and bare-metal recovery (BMR), and ships those recovery points to a Recovery Services vault. Enabling vault immutability with a 90-day window and soft delete protects the recovery points from deletion or modification — even by a Backup admin — for the immutability period. The MARS agent alone supports file/folder and system state but is more limited for application workloads, and Robocopy or Azure File Sync are replication tools, not backup, and provide no point-in-time recovery or ransomware-resistant immutability.

questions.question: You are migrating dozens of file servers from Windows Server 2012 R2 to Windows Server 2022. The migration must preserve NTFS permissions, local users and groups, shares, and the source server's identity (name and IP address) so that clients reconnect transparently, with minimal cutover downtime. Which tool is designed for this scenario?
options: Windows Server Migration Tools (SmigDeploy / Send-SmigServerData)
Storage Migration Service in Windows Admin Center
Distributed File System Replication (DFS-R) with a one-way connection
Robocopy with the /MIR /COPYALL /SECFIX switches
questions.explanation: Storage Migration Service (SMS) was built specifically to inventory, transfer, and cut over file servers. It copies files, ACLs, shares, local users and groups, and at cutover it can rename and re-IP the destination so it takes the identity of the source — clients keep using the same UNC paths without reconfiguration. SmigDeploy was retired with older Windows Server versions. DFS-R synchronises folders but does not move identity. Robocopy can copy data and ACLs but does not handle shares, local accounts, or identity cutover.

questions.question: Your team must lift-and-shift 60 on-premises VMware virtual machines to Azure with minimal downtime, including dependency analysis and right-sizing recommendations before the move. The migration plane must support agentless replication of the running VMs and a final cutover that boots the workloads as Azure VMs. Which Azure service is purpose-built for this?
options: Azure Site Recovery for cross-region Azure-to-Azure DR
Azure Migrate with the Discovery and assessment and Server Migration tools
Azure Data Box Heavy for offline bulk transfer
Azure Resource Mover
questions.explanation: Azure Migrate is the unified hub for datacentre migrations: the Discovery and assessment tool inventories VMware/Hyper-V/physical servers and produces Azure readiness and right-sizing reports, and the Server Migration tool performs agentless or agent-based replication of running VMs and a near-zero-downtime cutover into Azure. ASR can be used for some migrations but Azure Migrate is the recommended modern path and includes assessment. Data Box ships disks for petabyte-scale data transfer, not server migration. Azure Resource Mover moves resources between Azure regions after they are already in Azure.

questions.question: You want a single Azure pane of glass that ingests performance counters, Windows event logs, and security events from all your Arc-enabled Windows Server 2022 machines into a Log Analytics workspace so that you can query them with Kusto Query Language (KQL). Microsoft has consolidated the legacy MMA and Linux OMS agents into a single supported agent. Which agent should you deploy to those Arc-enabled servers?
options: The Microsoft Monitoring Agent (MMA / Log Analytics agent)
The Azure Diagnostics extension (WAD)
The Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) with Data Collection Rules
The Operations Manager (SCOM) management server agent
questions.explanation: The Azure Monitor Agent (AMA), driven by Data Collection Rules (DCRs), is the supported successor to the legacy Log Analytics / MMA / OMS agents. Microsoft has retired the Log Analytics agent for new deployments; AMA is the agent that ships data — event logs, performance counters, Sysmon, IIS logs, etc. — into a Log Analytics workspace for KQL queries and Sentinel ingestion, and it works on Azure VMs and on Arc-enabled servers alike. WAD is for older Azure-IaaS diagnostics. SCOM is on-premises monitoring, not an Azure Monitor agent.

questions.question: Users intermittently fail to authenticate against a Windows Server 2022 application that uses Kerberos. You suspect duplicate Service Principal Names (SPNs) for the service account. Which built-in command-line tool will list, add, remove, or query duplicate SPNs registered in Active Directory?
options: dcdiag.exe
nltest.exe
setspn.exe
repadmin.exe
questions.explanation: setspn.exe is the supported tool for managing SPNs in Active Directory. setspn -X searches the entire forest for duplicate SPNs (a classic cause of Kerberos failures), setspn -L lists SPNs for an account, and setspn -A / -D add or remove them. dcdiag tests domain controller health, nltest queries secure channels and trusts, and repadmin diagnoses AD replication. None of those three manage SPNs.

questions.question: You are tightening administrative access to a tier-0 Windows Server 2022 jump host. Operators currently have local Administrators group membership, but auditors require that they only get the specific cmdlets they need to do their job, on demand, with their actions logged and their session run under a temporary virtual account that has no persistent privileges. Which Windows Server feature should you implement?
options: Restricted Groups defined in a Group Policy Object
Just Enough Administration (JEA) using PowerShell session configurations and role capability files
Authentication Policies and Authentication Policy Silos
User Rights Assignment policies set to deny network logon
questions.explanation: Just Enough Administration (JEA) was designed for exactly this scenario. You define role capability files that whitelist the cmdlets, functions, and providers an operator may run, register a constrained PowerShell session configuration, and connections to that endpoint execute under a per-session virtual account that exists only for the lifetime of the session. Every command is transcribed and logged. Restricted Groups manage who is in a local group but do not constrain what they can run. Authentication Policy Silos restrict where credentials can be used, not which cmdlets are exposed. User Rights Assignment changes broad logon rights, not application-level command scope.

questions.question: Your file server cluster reports the cluster service is degraded and intermittently evicts a node. You need to collect a full cluster log including event-time-correlated entries for every node in a time window, written to a folder you control, for opening a Microsoft support case. Which PowerShell cmdlet collects that diagnostic bundle?
options: Get-ClusterLog -Destination C:\Temp
Test-Cluster -ReportName ValidationReport
Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-FailoverClustering/Operational'
Show-ClusterPerformanceHistory
questions.explanation: Get-ClusterLog generates the per-node cluster.log file (and writes it to the path supplied with -Destination) that Microsoft support engineers expect when diagnosing failover cluster issues — it dumps the in-memory tracing buffer with event-time correlation. Test-Cluster runs the cluster validation suite, useful before deployment but it does not collect a runtime log. Get-WinEvent only retrieves the operational channel and misses the cluster's in-memory trace. Show-ClusterPerformanceHistory is for S2D performance metrics, not diagnostics.
